\chapter{Comen and Viven --- Agreeing Again}
\label{ch:spanish-er-ir-3pl}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what they eat and what they live, with one ending shared by both families.}

After two chapters apart the families fall back into step and stay there.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comen · viven]{comen and viven — agreeing again}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-comen-viven}



\begin{quote}
What is \textquotedblleft{}they speak\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Hablan}.) And who else does that form address? (\emph{Ustedes}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending for both}]
Both families take \textbf{-en}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{comen} — \emph{they eat}, \emph{ustedes} eat. \textbf{viven} — \emph{they live}, \emph{ustedes} live.
\end{quote}

No split here. After two chapters of divergence the families fall back into step, and they stay there.

That is the shape of the whole system, and it is worth holding as one sentence:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{-er\emph{ and }-ir\emph{ are identical in four of the six slots. They differ only in }nosotros\emph{ and }vosotros\emph{.\textbf{}}}}
\end{quote}

Two exceptions in a system of twelve forms. You have now met both, and everything else you already knew.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comen, viven\textquotedblright{} — one ending, both families
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ustedes comen\textquotedblright{}, addressing a group
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \emph{they eat} and \emph{they live}. (\textbf{Comen}, \textbf{viven}.) In how many of the six slots do the two families agree? (\textbf{Four}.) Next chapter: all three families, whole.
\end{tcolorbox}
